title: 2 Samuel 5:1–5
context: 2 Samuel 5:1–5 tells how all the tribes of Israel come to David at Hebron after the deaths of Saul, Abner, and Ish-bosheth. They acknowledge kinship with him, his earlier military leadership, and the LORD’s word that he would shepherd Israel. The elders make a covenant with David before the LORD and anoint him king over all Israel. The narrator adds his age and the length of his reign. Arminian and Reformed readers share the reading that God’s promise to David (1 Samuel 16:1–13) is fulfilled in his timing, through a covenant made with the people’s free consent.

verses.text: Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and spoke, saying, “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh.
verses.arminianNotes: All the tribes come to David at Hebron and say, "We are your bone and your flesh." Arminian readers see the tribes freely recognizing David as their king, and they note that the long civil war ends through the people’s own choice to unite under him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the tribes are coming at last to the king God had chosen years before. Both traditions read the verse as God bringing his promise about David to fulfillment through human decisions, without forcing the people.

verses.text: In times past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led Israel out and in. The LORD said to you, ‘You will be shepherd of my people Israel, and you will be prince over Israel.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The tribes recall that David led Israel’s armies under Saul and that the LORD said he would shepherd Israel and be prince over it. Arminians see the people acknowledging both David’s proven leadership and God’s word, a fitting basis for a covenant king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the shepherd image becomes central in later Scripture, including the promise of a Davidic shepherd (Ezekiel 34:23). Both traditions read the verse as joining God’s call and the people’s recognition.

verses.text: So all the elders of Israel came to the king to Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the LORD; and they anointed David king over Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The elders come to Hebron, David makes a covenant with them before the LORD, and they anoint him king over Israel. Arminian readers see a covenant with mutual obligations, in which the king serves under God and the people commit themselves to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that this is David’s third anointing, after 1 Samuel 16:13 and 2 Samuel 2:4. Both traditions see the kingship placed "before the LORD," under his authority, and read the covenant as shaping the king’s responsibility to the people.

verses.text: David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years.
verses.arminianNotes: David was thirty when he began to reign and reigned forty years. Arminians see the note as marking David’s patience in waiting many years after his anointing before receiving the throne, trusting God’s timing rather than seizing power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the chronology as the narrator’s formal summary of a reign under God’s providence. Both traditions note that the forty-year figure appears in the summary of his reign in 1 Kings 2:11.

verses.text: In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: David reigned in Hebron over Judah for seven years and six months, then in Jerusalem for thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah. Arminian readers see the step-by-step growth of his rule as the way God fulfilled his promise through real historical process.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the distinction between Judah and Israel, which anticipates the later division of the kingdom. Both traditions read the verse as historical summary that sets the stage for the move to Jerusalem.
